block.title: Rising through black water, breaking the surface into sunrise
block.positive: SNES-era 16-bit pixel art inspired concept rendering, bold dark outlines, saturated limited palette, vertical-feel composition inside a widescreen frame, subtle CRT scanline glow; ending scene painted at hi-resolution, sacred quiet, ultra-detailed large-format art with pixel-art texture accents. The boundary of worlds, seen from just under it: the bottom two-thirds of the frame are black water — deep, still, absolute — fading from midnight teal at the top of the depths to the faintest blue-black at the very bottom, crossed only by one long column of rising silver bubbles that trails off-frame below, the flight path of the ship that climbed all the way out of the abyss. The top one-third is air at first light, and the two worlds meet along a trembling silver ceiling: from beneath, the surface is a hammered mirror arched open in the center where a battered manta-shaped fighter — pale mint ray-wings, a green canopy now dark, twin thrusters guttering a last lazy halo of bubbles — has just punched through and is hanging at the apex of its break, shedding curtains of glowing water off every wing edge, each falling droplet catching the sunrise like a dropped bead of lamp-glass. Beyond and above, the real sky: a thin band of deep navy at the frame's upper corners melting into a huge, unhurried sunrise of pale gold and rose along the open sea-horizon, the sun itself just topping the line, its light laying a road of shimmer straight under the risen ship. Nothing hostile exists in this image. The palette is teal-black depths against gold-rose dawn, lifted navy shadows, never pure black. No text, no letters, no UI.

block.notes: Manta reference: hull pale mint #c8e0d0, canopy green #40d070, thrusters amber — here dimmed, engine-lights almost out; depths teal #16485a fading to navy-black. Half-submerged ship at the surface is the hard ask — models want the ship either flying or sunk, so "hanging at the apex of its break, shedding curtains of water" is load-bearing. Bubble column entering from below sells the nine-thousand-meter climb without showing it.
